section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: Cortes's actions in the passage most directly continue which earlier Iberian tradition?

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"In these chapels are the images or idols... the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints... I answered, through the interpreters, that they were deceived in expecting any favors from idols, the work of their own hands... and that they must learn there was but one God, the universal Lord of all, who had created the heavens and earth, and all things else, and had made them and us."
—Hernando Cortés, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520 (abridged)

options: A. The Portuguese policy of peaceful coastal trading in Asia
B. The Reconquista, in which Christian rulers framed war against non-Christians as holy struggle
C. The Spanish Inquisition's persecution of conversos within Spain
D. Columbus's commercial search for a westward route to Asia
items.explanation: Cortés smashing Aztec idols and planting images of the Virgin and saints continues the Reconquista — the centuries-long Iberian campaign in which Christian rulers framed war against non-Christians as holy struggle. Like the crusading knights who retook Spain from Muslim rule, Cortés presented conquest as God's work: purifying polluted temples and replacing false gods with the true faith. The conquistador was the Reconquista's heir.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Portuguese peaceful trading in Asia was a different, commercial model — not Cortés's holy war.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Cortés's idol-smashing continues the Reconquista tradition of framing war against non-Christians as holy struggle.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Inquisition persecuted conversos within Spain; Cortés waged war abroad.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Columbus's commercial search for Asia was about trade routes, not holy war against idolatry.

items.stem: The fact that this letter was addressed to Charles V best helps explain which feature of the document?

stimulus.image_caption: Hernan Cortes introducing Christianity, from the Lienzo de Tlaxcala (c. 1550s; 1773 copy).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Copy (1773, Manuel de Yllanez) of the c.1550s Lienzo de Tlaxcala; pre-1930
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"In these chapels are the images or idols... the principal ones, in which the people have greatest faith and confidence, I precipitated from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints... I answered, through the interpreters, that they were deceived in expecting any favors from idols, the work of their own hands... and that they must learn there was but one God, the universal Lord of all, who had created the heavens and earth, and all things else, and had made them and us."
—Hernando Cortés, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520 (abridged)

options: A. Its portrayal of the expedition as loyal service to crown and church
B. Its scrupulous neutrality between Spanish and Aztec perspectives
C. Its criticism of the Spanish crown's colonial policies
D. Its argument that Native peoples should govern themselves
items.explanation: Cortés wrote to Charles V — his king and the font of all authority for the expedition — so the letter is crafted to please its reader: it portrays the conquest as loyal service to crown and church, with Cortés as the faithful servant extending Christendom and royal dominion. The addressee explains the document's flattering frame; Cortés was justifying his unauthorized expedition to the man who could punish or reward him.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Addressed to Charles V, the letter portrays the expedition as loyal service to crown and church.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The letter is partisan Spanish propaganda, not neutral between perspectives.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Cortés does not criticize the crown's colonial policies; he seeks its favor.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The letter does not argue for Native self-government; it celebrates their subjugation.

items.stem: Bradford's history is best characterized as

stimulus.text:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following excerpt.

"Squanto... was a special instrument sent of God for their good beyond their expectation. He directed them how to set their corn, where to take fish, and to procure other commodities, and was also their pilot to bring them to unknown places for their profit, and never left them till he died."
—William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation (abridged)

options: A. A Loyalist polemic against the Revolution
B. A Federalist essay on constitutional government
C. A transcendentalist meditation on nature
D. A firsthand Puritan chronicle of history and providence
items.explanation: William Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation is a firsthand Puritan chronicle: written by the colony's governor from lived experience, recording events as the working of divine providence. Squanto as God's special instrument is the book's method — history read as Providence's story. It is neither Loyalist polemic nor philosophy; it is a Puritan's eyewitness account of God's dealings with His people.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Bradford wrote in the 1600s, a century before the Revolution; no Loyalist polemic was possible.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The history is not a Federalist constitutional essay.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century movement, not Bradford's Puritan chronicle.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Bradford's history is a firsthand Puritan chronicle of history and providence.

(C) {'letter': 'C', 'text': 'The English'}
(D) {'letter': 'D', 'text': 'The Dutch'}
items.explanation: France's Fort Caroline in Florida (1564) was destroyed by the Spanish under Pedro Menéndez de Avilés in 1565 — Spain would tolerate no French Protestant foothold in lands it claimed. Menéndez massacred the Huguenot colonists and founded St. Augustine. European rivalry, not Native resistance, ended the French settlement.

items.stem: The Navigation Acts contributed most directly to which development in the colonies?

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the increase of shipping and encouragement of the navigation of this nation, wherein, under the good providence and protection of God, the wealth, safety, and strength of this kingdom is so much concerned... no goods or commodities whatsoever shall be imported into or exported out of any lands... belonging to his Majesty... but in such ships as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of England..."
—Navigation Act of 1660 (abridged)

options: A. The rapid industrialization of the New England economy
B. The abolition of the transatlantic slave trade
C. Widespread smuggling and growing resentment of imperial trade regulation
D. Colonial satisfaction with Parliament's economic stewardship
items.explanation: The Navigation Acts forced colonial trade into English ships and through English ports, raising costs and limiting markets. Colonists responded with widespread smuggling — John Hancock's fortune was built on it — and with growing resentment of imperial trade regulation. The acts taught colonists to evade and hate Parliament's economic control.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The acts did not industrialize New England; they restricted its trade.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The acts did not abolish the slave trade; they regulated commerce.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Navigation Acts produced widespread smuggling and resentment of imperial trade regulation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Colonists resented, not applauded, Parliament's economic stewardship.

items.stem: The Salem trials' collapse in 1692–93 was hastened when Pyle's 1883 illustration above depicts a witchcraft arrest of the kind that swept Salem.

stimulus.pd_rationale: Howard Pyle, 1883; pre-1930 publication
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"That whereas your poor and humble petitioner being condemned to die, do humbly beg of you to take it into your judicious and pious considerations that your poor and humble petitioners may be acquitted..."
—Mary Easty, petition from Salem jail, 1692 (abridged)

options: A. England dispatched troops to restore order
B. Spectral evidence was discredited and accusations reached the elite
C. The colony adopted an English bill of rights
D. Cotton Mather was executed for witchcraft
items.explanation: The Salem trials collapsed when the evidentiary basis crumbled: spectral evidence — testimony that a specter afflicted the victim — was discredited, and accusations began reaching the colony's elite, including the governor's wife. When the panic threatened the powerful, it ended. The trials died not from mercy but from the elite's self-protection.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. England sent no troops to end the trials; the colony ended them itself.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The trials' collapse was hastened when spectral evidence was discredited and accusations reached the elite.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. No English bill of rights was adopted to end the trials.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Cotton Mather was not executed; he survived and defended the trials.

items.stem: The group that Williams criticizes in the excerpt would have been most likely to settle which of these regions of the American colonies?

stimulus.text: “I observe the great and wonderful mistake, both our own and our fathers, as to the civil powers of this world, acting in spiritual matters. I have read…the last will and testament of the Lord Jesus over many times, and yet I cannot find by one tittle of that testament that if He had been pleased to have accepted of a temporal crown and government that ever He would have put forth the least finger of temporal or civil power in the matters of His spiritual affairs and Kingdom. Hence must it lamentably be against the testimony of Christ Jesus for the civil state to impose upon the souls of the people a religion, a worship, a ministry, oaths (in religious and civil affairs), tithes, times, days, marryings, and buryings in holy ground….” Source: Roger Williams, The Hireling Ministry None of Christ’s, 1652

options: (A) The southern Colonies
(B) The New England Colonies
(C) The Middle Colonies
(D) The Chesapeake Colonies
items.explanation: Roger Williams denounces the civil state's imposition of religion — forcing worship, ministry, oaths, and tithes on people's souls. The group he criticizes is the Massachusetts Puritan establishment, which fused church and state and banished dissenters like Williams himself. His critique targets the New England colonies' theocratic order.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Southern colonies were Anglican, not the theocratic order Williams attacked.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Williams criticizes the New England colonies' imposition of religion by civil power.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Middle Colonies were more tolerant; Williams's target was Massachusetts.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Chesapeake colonies were not the theocracy Williams denounced.

items.stem: The document above was most likely written for all of the following reasons EXCEPT

stimulus.text: “After an unequivocal experience of the inefficiency of the subsisting federal government, you are called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America. The subject speaks its own importance; comprehending in its consequences nothing less than the existing of the union, the safety and welfare of the parts of which it is composed, the fate of an empire in many respects the most interesting in the world. It has been frequently remarked that it seems to have been reserved to the people of this country, by their conduct and example, to decide the important question, whether societies of men are really capable or not of establishing good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend for their political constitutions on accident and force. If there be any truth in the remark, the crisis at which we are arrived may with propriety be regarded as the era in which that decision is to be made; and a wrong election of the part we shall act may, in this view, deserve to be considered as the general misfortune of mankind.” Source: The Federalist Papers , 1788

options: (A) to expand the national political franchise
(B) to create a government that could more easily respond to internal rebellions
(C) to make it easier for the federal government to raise tax revenue
(D) to protect the interests of political elites
items.explanation: The Federalist Papers were written to win ratification of the Constitution — to create a government that could handle rebellions, raise revenue, and protect elite interests. Expanding the national political franchise was never their purpose; the founders feared too much democracy, not too little. The Papers argue for energetic government, not for broader voting rights.

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The Federalist Papers were not written to expand the political franchise.
option_explanations.B: The Papers were written for this, so it is not the answer. Shays's Rebellion proved the need for a government that could respond.
option_explanations.C: The Papers were written for this, so it is not the answer. Taxation power was central to the new Constitution.
option_explanations.D: The Papers were written for this, so it is not the answer. Protecting property and elite interests motivated the framers.

items.stem: Jefferson was responding to what situation?

stimulus.image_caption: 'Ograbme, or the American Snapping-Turtle,' embargo cartoon, 1807.
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 1-4 refer to the cartoon above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: A. French aggression under Napoleon
B. British interference with American shipping
C. British support for western Indians
D. Domestic electoral losses
items.explanation: Jefferson's embargo — the image's context — was his response to British interference with American shipping: impressment of sailors, seizures of cargo, and violations of neutral rights during the Napoleonic Wars. Unable to fight Britain, Jefferson tried economic coercion instead. The embargo was the answer to Britain's maritime bullying.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. French aggression was not the embargo's target; British maritime practices were.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Jefferson was responding to British interference with American shipping.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. British support for western Indians was a grievance, but not the embargo's cause.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Domestic electoral losses did not prompt the embargo.

items.stem: In the passage, Dickinson's phrase 'perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty' refers to

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"A perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty, is absolutely requisite in all free states. The very texture of their constitution, in mixed government, demands it... Let us take care of our rights, and we therein take care of our prosperity."
—John Dickinson, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, 1767–1768 (abridged)

options: A. Envy of Britain's commercial wealth
B. Suspicion of the other American colonies
C. Constant vigilance by the people against encroachments on their rights
D. Hostility toward all forms of government
items.explanation: Dickinson's perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty is his call for constant vigilance by the people against encroachments on their rights. In a mixed government, he argues, liberty survives only if citizens jealously guard it — watching Parliament, watching power, never trusting authority to respect rights unprompted. Jealousy here means watchfulness, not envy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Jealousy does not mean envy of Britain's wealth; it means vigilance for liberty.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Dickinson does not counsel suspicion of other colonies; he counsels vigilance against power.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The phrase means constant vigilance by the people against encroachments on their rights.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Dickinson does not preach hostility to all government; he preaches guarding liberty within it.

items.stem: Washington's letter was written most directly in response to which of the following? The illustration above shows Shays's rebels fleeing at Springfield in 1787 — the domestic unrest Washington feared the Confederation could not suppress.

stimulus.image_caption: Shays's rebels fleeing Continental troops at the Springfield arsenal, January 1787 (illustration, c. 1902).
stimulus.pd_rationale: C. Kendrick, c.1902; pre-1930 publication
stimulus.text_stimulus: "We have errors to correct. We have probably had too good an opinion of human nature in forming our confederation. Experience has taught us that men will not adopt and carry into execution measures the best calculated for their own good without the intervention of a coercive power. I do not conceive that we can exist long as a nation without having lodged somewhere a power which will pervade the whole Union in as energetic a manner as the authority of the state governments extends over the several states.... What a triumph for the advocates of despotism to find that we are incapable of governing ourselves, and that systems founded on the basis of equal liberty are merely ideal and fallacious." — George Washington to John Jay, August 1, 1786

options: (A) Parliament's passage of the Coercive Acts closing the port of Boston.
(B) Disputes among the states over the terms of the Treaty of Paris.
(C) The outbreak of revolution in France and its threat to American trade.
(D) The Confederation Congress's inability to raise revenue, pay its debts, or suppress domestic unrest.
items.explanation: Washington's letter on Shays's Rebellion — his alarm that commotions gather strength like snowballs — was written most directly in response to the Confederation Congress's inability to raise revenue, pay its debts, or suppress domestic unrest. Massachusetts couldn't crush the rebellion without help, and Congress couldn't help. The letter is the Confederation's weakness made personal.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Coercive Acts were 1774, a decade before this letter.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Treaty of Paris disputes were not the letter's subject; domestic impotence was.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The French Revolution came in 1789, after the letter.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Washington wrote in response to the Confederation's inability to raise revenue, pay debts, or suppress unrest.

items.stem: The political party of the early 1800s most associated with the document above supported which of the following views?

stimulus.text: “After an unequivocal experience of the inefficiency of the subsisting federal government, you are called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America. The subject speaks its own importance; comprehending in its consequences nothing less than the existing of the union, the safety and welfare of the parts of which it is composed, the fate of an empire in many respects the most interesting in the world. It has been frequently remarked that it seems to have been reserved to the people of this country, by their conduct and example, to decide the important question, whether societies of men are really capable or not of establishing good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend for their political constitutions on accident and force. If there be any truth in the remark, the crisis at which we are arrived may with propriety be regarded as the era in which that decision is to be made; and a wrong election of the part we shall act may, in this view, deserve to be considered as the general misfortune of mankind.” Source: The Federalist Papers , 1788

options: (A) A national bank was necessary to encourage foreign investment and maintain national economic security.
(B) The provisions of the U.S. Constitution should be applied strictly as written.
(C) The French Revolution would result in a more just form of government with more governance provided to the people.
(D) Agriculture and farming are the backbone of the American economy.
items.explanation: The Federalist Papers were the Federalist Party's founding document, and the early-1800s Federalists supported Hamilton's program: a national bank to encourage investment and secure the nation's economy. The bank was the Federalist economic creed — energetic government promoting national prosperity. Strict construction, Francophilia, and agrarianism belonged to their Jeffersonian opponents.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Federalists supported a national bank for investment and economic security.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Strict construction was the Democratic-Republican position, not the Federalists'.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Federalists feared the French Revolution; they did not celebrate it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Agrarianism was Jefferson's creed, not the Federalists'.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the Boston Massacre is true? Revere's 1770 engraving above depicts the Boston Massacre — the violence whose underlying tensions the question asks about.

stimulus.image_caption: Paul Revere, 'The Bloody Massacre perpetrated in King-Street Boston on March 5th 1770' (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Paul Revere, 1770; Library of Congress, pre-1930

options: (A) Several of the soldiers involved were imprisoned without trial, which increased British animosity toward the colonists.
(B) The shootings were essentially unprovoked, which increased American animosity toward the British.
(C) The Quartering Act of 1765 was largely responsible for the underlying tensions that ultimately led to violence.
(D) The incident led to immediate calls for war by most political leaders on both sides of the conflict.
items.explanation: The Boston Massacre's underlying tensions came from the British military occupation of Boston — troops quartered among civilians under the Quartering Act of 1765, competing for jobs, brawling in the streets. The soldiers who fired were part of an occupying force the town resented. The Quartering Act's imposition of troops on the city created the tinder; March 5, 1770 was the spark.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The soldiers were tried — John Adams defended them — not imprisoned without trial.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The shootings followed days of provocation and brawls; they were not simply unprovoked.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Quartering Act of 1765 created the underlying tensions that led to violence.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Few leaders called for war in 1770; the incident was exploited, not escalated to war.

items.stem: A major weakness of the national government referenced above was that it

stimulus.text: “Permit us, then, earnestly to recommend these articles to the immediate and dispassionate attention of the legislatures of the respective states. Let them be candidly reviewed under a sense of the difficulty of combining in one system the various sentiments and interests of a continent divided into so many sovereign and independent communities, under a conviction of the absolute necessity of uniting all our councils and all our strength, to maintain and defend our common liberties….” Source: Journals of the Continental Congress, 1777

options: (A) created a too-powerful chief executive
(B) did not include a mechanism for their own amendment
(C) made it too difficult for the government to raise money through taxes and duties
(D) denied the federal government the power to mediate disputes between states
items.explanation: The Articles of Confederation's fatal flaw was fiscal: Congress could not tax but had to request funds from the states, which often refused. A government that cannot raise money cannot pay debts, maintain armies, or function. The Articles made it too difficult for the government to raise money through taxes and duties — the weakness that defined the Confederation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Articles created no powerful executive; that was the complaint's opposite.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Articles did include an amendment mechanism, however cumbersome.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Articles' major weakness was the inability to raise money through taxes and duties.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Congress could mediate state disputes; it lacked enforcement power.

items.stem: Regarding adoption and ratification of the U.S. Constitution, the writer of the excerpt above would be most likely to agree with which of the following statements?

stimulus.text: “After an unequivocal experience of the inefficiency of the subsisting federal government, you are called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America. The subject speaks its own importance; comprehending in its consequences nothing less than the existing of the union, the safety and welfare of the parts of which it is composed, the fate of an empire in many respects the most interesting in the world. It has been frequently remarked that it seems to have been reserved to the people of this country, by their conduct and example, to decide the important question, whether societies of men are really capable or not of establishing good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend for their political constitutions on accident and force. If there be any truth in the remark, the crisis at which we are arrived may with propriety be regarded as the era in which that decision is to be made; and a wrong election of the part we shall act may, in this view, deserve to be considered as the general misfortune of mankind.” Source: The Federalist Papers , 1788

options: (A) A more established central government as proposed in the U.S. Constitution would lead to despotism and a possible return to monarchical rule.
(B) Adoption and ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution would result in the loss of states’ rights to self-govern.
(C) Failure to include adoption of a Bill of Rights along with the U.S. Constitution would result in loss of individual rights and threatened public liberties.
(D) The U.S. Constitution should be ratified and does not need an additional Bill of Rights.
items.explanation: The Federalist writer — Publius, arguing for ratification — believed the Constitution's checks and balances made a Bill of Rights unnecessary: the government's enumerated powers left rights secure. Federalists held that the Constitution should be ratified as written, without additional amendments. The Bill of Rights came only as the price of Anti-Federalist support.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Federalist writer favored the Constitution; despotism was the Anti-Federalist warning.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Loss of states' rights was the Anti-Federalist fear, not the Federalist position.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Demanding a Bill of Rights was the Anti-Federalist position.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Federalist writer held the Constitution should be ratified without an additional Bill of Rights.

items.stem: Dix's memorial was part of which broader antebellum movement?

stimulus.text:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following excerpt.

"I come to present the strong claims of suffering humanity. I come as the advocate of helpless, forgotten, insane, and idiotic men and women... I proceed, gentlemen, briefly to call your attention to the present state of insane persons confined within this Commonwealth, in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens! Chained, naked, beaten with rods, and lashed into obedience."
—Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843 (abridged)

options: A. The abolitionist movement against slavery
B. The temperance movement against alcohol
C. The common-school movement for public education
D. The asylum reform movement of the Second Great Awakening
items.explanation: Dorothea Dix's 1843 memorial — her investigation of abused insane persons in cages and cellars — belonged to the asylum reform movement, the Second Great Awakening's crusade to treat society's outcasts humanely. Like temperance and abolition, asylum reform grew from revivalist moral urgency: suffering was sin's consequence, and Christians must relieve it. Dix's memorial is perfectionist reform applied to the mentally ill.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Abolition fought slavery, not asylum abuse.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Temperance fought alcohol, not the treatment of the insane.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The common-school movement built public education, a different reform.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Dix's memorial was part of the Second Great Awakening's asylum reform movement.

items.stem: Brook Farm in Massachusetts, the Oneida Community in upstate New York, and New Harmony in Indiana were similar in that they

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photographed c.1865-1875 (Moulton & Dopp). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) were religious communities inspired by the Second Great Awakening
(B) demonstrated the attraction of communism to many Americans
(C) failed because they practiced political and social equality within their own communities
(D) were utopian communities designed to ameliorate the effects of a growing commercial society
items.explanation: Brook Farm, Oneida, and New Harmony — despite their differences — were all utopian communities: experimental societies designed to ameliorate the effects of a growing commercial society. Their founders believed industrial capitalism corrupted human relations and that small, intentional communities could model a better way. Utopianism was the era's answer to the market revolution's discontents.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Not all were religious communities; New Harmony was secular and Owenite.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Communism as a doctrine had little to do with these American experiments.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. They did not fail because they practiced equality; many failed for economic and personal reasons.
option_explanations.D: Correct. They were utopian communities designed to ameliorate commercial society's effects.

items.stem: Which of the following was most directly an effect of the religious movement Finney led?
options: (A) The founding of socialist utopian communes.
(B) The political drive for western territorial expansion in the 1840s and 1850s.
(C) The growth of reform movements such as temperance and abolition.
(D) The removal of Native communities from the Southeast.
items.explanation: Charles Finney's revivals — the burned-over district's great awakenings — converted thousands and then sent them into reform: temperance societies, abolitionist organizations, moral reform crusades. Finney taught that converted sinners must perfect society, and his converts became the foot soldiers of antebellum reform. The revivals' most direct effect was the growth of reform movements.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Socialist communes were Owenite experiments, not Finney's revival product.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Western expansion was political, not the revivals' direct effect.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Finney's movement most directly produced the growth of reform movements like temperance and abolition.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Native removal was federal policy, not a revival consequence.

items.stem: Which of the following represents a consequence of the ideology expressed by the author above between 1800 and 1865?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Painted 1872 by John Gast (d. 1896). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) Debates over the expansion of slavery intensified.
(B) New religious denominations such as Mormonism emerged.
(C) Women began organizing more explicitly around political causes such as temperance and suffrage.
(D) Politicians argued for increased tariffs to protect nascent American industry.
items.explanation: The ideology in the image — presumably Manifest Destiny — had as its great consequence the intensification of debates over slavery's expansion between 1800 and 1865. Every new territory acquired in the name of destiny forced the question: slave or free? Manifest Destiny made expansion inevitable and the slavery question unavoidable.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The ideology's consequence was intensified debates over the expansion of slavery.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Mormonism's emergence was a religious development, not Manifest Destiny's consequence.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Women's political organizing grew from reform movements, not from expansionist ideology.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Tariff debates were economic, not the direct consequence of expansionist ideology.

items.stem: According to the passage, Tecumseh's view of Native land ownership was that

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"Brother, since the peace was made, you have killed some of the Shawnees, Winnebagoes, Delawares, and Miamis, and you have taken our land from us... The way, and the only way, to check and to stop this evil, is for all the red men to unite in claiming a common and equal right in the land."
—Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, 1810 (abridged)

options: A. Land belonged to all Native peoples in common, so no chief could sell it
B. Each tribe owned its own territory absolutely
C. Tribal land should be sold to the highest bidder
D. The British crown held title to all Native land
items.explanation: Tecumseh told Harrison that the land belonged to all red men in common — that no single chief or tribe could sell what belonged to everyone. His pan-Indian vision rejected the American practice of buying land from isolated chiefs: the soil was a common inheritance, and only all tribes together could dispose of it. Common ownership was the foundation of his confederacy.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Tecumseh held that land belonged to all Native peoples in common, so no chief could sell it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Absolute tribal ownership was the opposite of Tecumseh's common-right doctrine.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Selling to the highest bidder was the American system Tecumseh opposed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The British crown's title was not Tecumseh's view; common Native ownership was.

items.stem: The writers who produced the Lowell Offering were which of the following groups?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1840-1860 (Popular Graphic Arts, Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) New England abolitionists active in the Second Great Awakening.
(B) Young women employed as textile operatives in Lowell's early factories.
(C) Transcendentalist writers at the Brook Farm commune.
(D) Free Black women in Massachusetts following the state's gradual elimination of slavery.
items.explanation: The Lowell Offering — the literary magazine of poems, stories, and essays — was written by the young women employed as textile operatives in Lowell's early factories: the famous mill girls. Farm daughters turned factory workers, they wrote about their labor, their lives, and their longings. The Offering is the voice of America's first female industrial workforce.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. New England abolitionists were a different group; the Offering's writers were mill operatives.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Lowell Offering was written by young women employed as textile operatives.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Brook Farm transcendentalists were intellectuals, not mill girls.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Free Black women were not the Offering's authors.

items.stem: The most direct effect of the situation described above involved the creation of which of the following political parties?

stimulus.text: “Mr. Adams is the Constitutional President and as such I would myself be the last man in the Commonwealth to oppose him upon any other ground than that of principle…. As to his character also, it is hardly necessary for me to observe, that I had esteemed him as a virtuous, able and honest man; and when rumor was stamping the sudden union of his and the friends of Mr. Clay with intrigue, barter and bargain I did not, nay, I could not believe that Mr. Adams participated in a management deserving such epithets…. But when these strange rumors became facts, when the predicted stipulation was promptly fulfilled, and Mr. Clay was Secretary of State, the inference was irresistible—I could not doubt the facts. It was well known that during the canvass Mr. Clay had denounced him as an apostate, as one of the most dangerous men in the union, and the last man in it that ought to be brought into the executive chair.” Source: Andrew Jackson, in a letter to Henry Lee, 1825

options: (A) The American Party
(B) The Democratic Party
(C) The Whig Party
(D) The Free-Soil Party
items.explanation: Jackson's 1825 letter fuming about the corrupt bargain — Clay's alleged deal making Adams president in exchange for the State Department — describes the grievance that created the Democratic Party. Jackson's supporters organized around their hero's wronged cause, building the mass party that would elect him in 1828. The corrupt-bargain charge was the Democrats' founding myth.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The American Party (Know-Nothings) came in the 1850s, from nativism, not the corrupt bargain.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The corrupt-bargain controversy most directly created the Democratic Party.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Whigs formed in opposition to Jackson, not from his grievance.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Free-Soil Party came in 1848, over slavery extension.

items.stem: Which of the following provides the best explanation for why Radical Republicans opposed Lincoln in 1861?
options: (A) Lincoln’s decision to issue the Emancipation Proclamation was done without congressional oversight.
(B) The Radical Republicans wanted immediate emancipation of enslaved people, but Lincoln refused to cooperate.
(C) Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan provided no assurance of Black suffrage.
(D) Lincoln’s appointment of Andrew Johnson as vice president clashed with the Reconstruction goals of the Senate.
items.explanation: Radical Republicans opposed Lincoln in 1861 because they wanted immediate emancipation of enslaved people, and Lincoln refused to cooperate — insisting the war was for the Union, not abolition. To Radicals like Sumner and Stevens, Lincoln's caution was moral cowardice; to Lincoln, premature emancipation would lose the border states. The split was over timing and principle: now versus later.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Emancipation Proclamation came in 1863, not 1861.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Radicals wanted immediate emancipation in 1861; Lincoln refused.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Ten Percent Plan came in 1863, not 1861.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Johnson's vice-presidential nomination was 1864, not 1861.

items.stem: Vicksburg was a crucial Union victory because

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1863 (Popular Graphic Arts, Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: A. It reversed a string of Union defeats that year
B. It opened the road to Atlanta
C. It gave the Union control of the Mississippi River
D. It proved Lee could be beaten in the East
items.explanation: Vicksburg (July 1863) was crucial because its surrender gave the Union control of the Mississippi River — splitting the Confederacy in two and severing Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas from the eastern South. Grant's campaign took the great river fortress after a brilliant siege. The Mississippi became a Union highway, and the Confederacy was cut in half.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Vicksburg did not reverse a string of Union defeats; it was part of a turning tide.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Atlanta's road opened later, with Sherman's 1864 campaign.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Vicksburg gave the Union control of the Mississippi River.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Lee was beaten in the East at Gettysburg, not at Vicksburg.

items.stem: The excerpt from Frederick Douglass is most clearly an example of which of the following developments in the mid-19th century?

stimulus.text: “In one view the slaveholders have a decided advantage over all opposition. It is well to notice this advantage—the advantage of complete organization. They are organized; and yet were not at the pains of creating their organizations. The State governments, where the system of slavery exists, are complete slavery organizations. The church organizations in those States are equally at the service of slavery; while the Federal Government, with its army and navy, from the chief magistracy in Washington, to the Supreme Court, and thence to the chief marshalship at New York, is pledged to support, defend, and propagate the crying curse of human bondage. The pen, the purse, and the sword, are united against the simple truth, preached by humble men in obscure places.” Source: Frederick Douglass, “The Dred Scott Decision” (speech), 1857 (public domain).

options: (A) The gradual replacement of indentured servants with enslaved Africans
(B) The preservation of African culture through cultural adaptation
(C) Southern influence upon the federal government to defend the institution of slavery
(D) The success of abolitionists to sway majority public opinion
items.explanation: Douglass's 1857 speech describes a federal government — Congress, the courts, the army, the presidency — organized to defend slavery: the slave power's complete organization. His point is Southern influence upon the federal government: the South had captured national institutions and turned them into slavery's defenders. The excerpt is an indictment of the slave power's national reach.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The servant-to-slave transition was a seventeenth-century development, not Douglass's subject.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. African cultural preservation is not the excerpt's theme.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Douglass's excerpt exemplifies Southern influence upon the federal government to defend slavery.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Douglass laments abolitionism's weakness against organized power, not its success.

items.stem: Perry's expedition is best understood in the context of which broader development?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Painted 1854-1858 (Japanese scroll; British Museum). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) An expanding American economy seeking new Pacific markets.
(B) Rapidly shifting alliances among the great powers of Europe.
(C) Rising nativist opposition to immigration in the United States.
(D) The national debate over whether slavery should expand westward.
items.explanation: Commodore Perry's 1853–1854 expedition to Japan is best understood in the context of an expanding American economy seeking new Pacific markets. Whalers, China traders, and merchants wanted coaling stations and open ports; Japan was the door to Asia's commerce. Perry's gunboats served American commercial ambition — the economy's hunger for markets drove the diplomacy.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Perry's expedition belongs to the context of an expanding American economy seeking Pacific markets.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. European alliance shifts were not the expedition's context.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Nativist opposition to immigration was a domestic issue, unrelated to Perry.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The slavery-expansion debate was sectional politics, not the expedition's driver.

items.stem: Nast's cartoon most directly reflects the continuity of which of the following debates in U.S. history?

stimulus.text:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options: (A) {'letter': 'A', 'text': 'Debates over civil rights'}
(B) {'letter': 'B', 'text': 'Debates over the use of military power'}
(C) {'letter': 'C', 'text': 'Debates over gun control'}
(D) {'letter': 'D', 'text': 'Debates over the role of political parties'}
items.explanation: Nast's 1874 cartoon — the White League and Klan shaking hands over a skull while a Black family cowers — most directly reflects the continuity of debates over civil rights in American history. From Reconstruction through Jim Crow to the modern movement, the question of Black Americans' rights has recurred in every generation. Nast's image is one moment in that long, unfinished argument.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Nast's cartoon reflects the continuity of debates over civil rights.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Military power is not the cartoon's subject.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Gun control is an anachronistic reading of the 1874 cartoon.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The role of parties is not the cartoon's theme.

items.stem: Which battle gave Lincoln the victory he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photographed September 1862 by Alexander Gardner. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) Gettysburg
(B) Antietam
(C) Fort Sumter
(D) Harper’s Ferry
items.explanation: Lincoln needed a victory before issuing the Emancipation Proclamation — lest it look like desperation — and Antietam (September 1862) gave it to him. The bloodiest single day of the war stopped Lee's invasion of Maryland and let Lincoln present emancipation from strength. Five days later, the preliminary proclamation was announced.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Gettysburg was 1863, after the proclamation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Antietam gave Lincoln the victory he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Fort Sumter began the war in 1861.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Harper's Ferry was John Brown's 1859 raid.

items.stem: The citizenship reform Garrison advocates was ultimately enacted through which of the following?
options: (A) The Emancipation Proclamation (1863), which freed enslaved people in rebellious states.
(B) The Reconstruction Act of 1867.
(C) The ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment (1868).
(D) The Civil Rights Act of 1875.
items.explanation: William Lloyd Garrison demanded Black citizenship — and the reform was ultimately enacted through the Fourteenth Amendment (1868), which declared all persons born in the United States to be citizens. The amendment overruled Dred Scott and wrote Garrison's demand into the Constitution. Citizenship came not by proclamation or statute but by constitutional amendment.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Emancipation Proclamation freed slaves but did not grant citizenship.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Reconstruction Act set readmission terms; it did not enact citizenship.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Garrison's citizenship reform was enacted through the Fourteenth Amendment.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Civil Rights Act of 1875 was later struck down and did not establish citizenship.

items.stem: Which of the following was a confederate advantage during the Civil War?
options: (A) Greater familiarity with battlegrounds
(B) Better organized state governments
(C) Superior transportation systems
(D) A larger fighting force
items.explanation: The Confederacy's great advantage was fighting on its own ground: Southern soldiers knew the battlegrounds — the roads, rivers, and ridges — while Northern armies marched through unfamiliar country. Familiarity with the terrain aided defense, surprise, and maneuver. The South's home-field advantage was real, if ultimately insufficient.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Greater familiarity with battlegrounds was a Confederate advantage.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Confederate state governments were often chaotic, not better organized.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The South's transportation was inferior to the North's.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The North had the larger fighting force, not the South.

items.stem: The passage of the Pendleton Act was a direct result of the
options: (A) assassination of Abraham Lincoln
(B) failure of Reconstruction
(C) assassination of James A. Garfield
(D) Supreme Court decision in Plessy v. Ferguson
items.explanation: The Pendleton Civil Service Act (1883) — creating merit-based federal employment — was a direct result of the assassination of President James A. Garfield in 1881 by a disappointed office-seeker. Garfield's murder by a spoils-system fanatic shocked the nation into reform. The act replaced patronage with examinations: death produced the merit system.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Lincoln's assassination was 1865, eighteen years before Pendleton.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Reconstruction's failure was not the Pendleton Act's cause.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Garfield's assassination directly produced the Pendleton Act.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) came after the Pendleton Act and concerned segregation.

items.stem: Farmers prized railroad access but feared the railroads because

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photograph by A. J. Russell, 1869 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the illustration described below.

The famous 1869 photograph of the Golden Spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah: two locomotives face each other, their cowcatchers nearly touching, while railroad workers, officials, and a military band crowd around the tracks where the final spike joins the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines.

options: A. Railroads could seize farmland by eminent domain
B. Railroads favored cattle ranchers
C. Railroads brought immigrant waves to their lands
D. Railroads controlled farm profits through freight rates
items.explanation: Farmers prized railroad access — it carried their crops to market — but feared the railroads because the lines controlled farm profits through freight rates. As local monopolies, railroads could charge what they liked, and farmers had no alternative. The railroad was both lifeline and leech: essential for selling, ruinous in its pricing.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Eminent domain seizures were not the farmers' central fear.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Favoring ranchers was not the issue; freight rates were.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Immigrant waves were not the farmers' railroad grievance.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Farmers feared railroads because they controlled farm profits through freight rates.

items.stem: Critics of the Panama Canal project chiefly objected that
options: A. It would require two-ocean naval power
B. It would cost an outlandish sum
C. The U.S. used underhanded tactics to get the canal rights
D. It would require a permanent garrison in Panama
items.explanation: Critics of the Panama Canal project chiefly objected not to its cost or engineering but to how America got it: Theodore Roosevelt's underhanded tactics — encouraging Panama's revolt against Colombia, then signing a treaty with the new government before it had a legislature. The canal was a triumph of engineering built on a foundation of diplomatic sharp dealing. The objection was moral: America had stolen the canal zone.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Two-ocean naval power was an argument for the canal, not against it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Cost was debated, but the chief objection was to the underhanded methods.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Critics chiefly objected that the U.S. used underhanded tactics to get the canal rights.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. A permanent garrison was not the chief objection.

items.stem: The advantage Rice describes — railroads quietly charging Standard Oil less than its rivals — best illustrates which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1904 cartoon (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.
stimulus.text_stimulus: "I am but one of many victims of Rockefeller's colossal combination.... I established what was known as the Ohio Oil Works.... I found... that the Standard Oil Company was offering the same quality of oil at much lower prices than I could do — from one to three cents a gallon less than I could possibly sell it for. I sought for the reason and found that the railroads were in league with the Standard Oil concern at every point, giving it discriminating rates and privileges of all kinds as against myself and all outside competitors." — George Rice, 'How I Was Ruined by Rockefeller,' New York World, October 16, 1898

options: (A) How a dominant firm used secret rebates and special deals to undersell and crush smaller competitors.
(B) The effectiveness of federal regulation in equalizing railroad freight rates.
(C) The benefits of vertical consolidation from oil wells to retail sales.
(D) The decisive role of labor unions in setting oil prices.
items.explanation: Rice describes railroads quietly charging Standard Oil less than its rivals — secret rebates that let the trust undersell and crush smaller competitors. The advantage illustrates how a dominant firm used special deals to destroy competition: Standard Oil's low prices were not efficiency but favoritism. Rebates were the trust's hidden weapon.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The rebates illustrate how a dominant firm used secret deals to undersell and crush smaller competitors.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Federal regulation did not equalize rates; the rebates thrived in regulation's absence.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Vertical consolidation is a different practice; the advantage here was secret rebates.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Labor unions did not set oil prices; railroad favoritism did.

items.stem: All of the following from 1870 to 1900 could be used to support the claims advanced by the authors in the party platform EXCEPT

stimulus.text: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. We charge that the controlling influences dominating both these parties have permitted the existing dreadful conditions to develop without serious effort to prevent or restrain them. Neither do they now promise us any substantial reform. They have agreed together to ignore, in the coming campaign, every issue but one. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. They propose to sacrifice our homes, lives, and children on the altar of mammon; to destroy the multitude in order to secure corruption funds from the millionaires. “Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of ‘the plain people,’ with which class it originated. We assert our purposes to be identical with the purposes of the National Constitution; to form a more perfect union and establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty for ourselves and our posterity.” Source: Populist Party Platform, 1892

options: (A) the creation of civil service laws like the Pendleton Act
(B) courts’ interpretations of the Sherman Antitrust Act
(C) the existence of urban political machines like Tammany Hall
(D) railroad scandals like Credit Mobilier
items.explanation: The Populist platform charges that both parties permitted dreadful conditions without serious reform effort. Courts' gutting of the Sherman Act, Tammany Hall's corruption, and the Credit Mobilier scandal all support that indictment. The Pendleton Act does not: civil service reform was a genuine reform, contradicting the claim that no substantial reform was attempted. It is the exception that disproves the platform's sweeping charge.

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The Pendleton Act was genuine reform, contradicting the platform's claim of no reform effort.
option_explanations.B: This supports the platform's claims, so it is not the answer. Courts weakened antitrust enforcement.
option_explanations.C: This supports the platform's claims, so it is not the answer. Tammany embodied the corruption denounced.
option_explanations.D: This supports the platform's claims, so it is not the answer. Credit Mobilier was the era's great railroad scandal.

items.stem: Which of the following best represents a continuity with the sentiment expressed in the Opper cartoon?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Puck, 1880 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.

options: (A) Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founding Hull House (1889) to aid immigrants.
(B) The Know-Nothing Party's 1854 anti-immigrant platform.
(C) Attorney General Palmer's deportation raids during the 1920s Red Scare.
(D) The Johnson-Reed Immigration Act of 1924 establishing discriminatory national-origins quotas.
items.explanation: The Opper cartoon — presumably depicting immigrant suffering or the need for humane treatment — finds its continuity in Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founding Hull House in 1889 to aid immigrants. Both express the Progressive-era impulse to help rather than exclude newcomers: settlement houses and sympathetic cartoons belong to the same humane tradition.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Hull House's aid to immigrants continues the Opper cartoon's sympathetic sentiment.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Know-Nothings' anti-immigrant platform was the opposite sentiment.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Palmer's deportation raids persecuted immigrants; they do not continue the cartoon's sympathy.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Johnson-Reed Act restricted immigration; it contradicts the cartoon's sentiment.

items.stem: Addams's approach at Hull House differed from earlier charity models by

stimulus.text:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

"At a meeting of working girls held at Hull House during a strike in a large shoe factory, the discussions made it clear that the strikers who had been most easily frightened were those who had no one to stand by them..."
—Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull House, 1910 (abridged)

options: A. Giving direct cash payments to striking workers
B. Lobbying Congress for open immigration
C. Settling in the neighborhood and supporting workers' own organizations
D. Running settlement workers for political office
items.explanation: Jane Addams's innovation was the settlement itself: Hull House workers lived in the immigrant neighborhood, learned its needs from the inside, and supported workers' own organizations — like the striking shoe-factory girls — rather than dispensing charity from above. Earlier charity models gave alms or moral lectures; Addams gave solidarity. Settlement meant standing with workers, not over them.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Hull House did not give direct cash payments to strikers; it offered organizing space and support.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Addams did not lobby Congress for open immigration.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Addams settled in the neighborhood and supported workers' own organizations.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Settlement workers did not run for political office as a method.

items.stem: The 'Share Our Wealth' plan's funding mechanism relied on

stimulus.text:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following excerpt.

Senator Huey Long charged that a tiny elite hoarded the nation's wealth while millions suffered in the Depression. He proposed capping personal fortunes, guaranteeing every family a homestead and a minimum annual income, shortening the workweek, and providing free college and old-age pensions — all funded by steep taxes on the rich.
—After Huey P. Long, 'Share Our Wealth' radio address, February 1934 (paraphrased)

options: A. Confiscatory taxation of large fortunes and inheritances
B. Maintaining a strictly balanced federal budget
C. Borrowing through foreign loans from European creditors
D. Returning the nation to the gold standard
items.explanation: Huey Long's Share Our Wealth plan funded its promises — homesteads, guaranteed incomes, free college, old-age pensions — through confiscatory taxation of large fortunes and inheritances: capping personal wealth and seizing the surplus for redistribution. Soak the rich was the mechanism; every family's security would come from the fortunes of the few.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Share Our Wealth relied on confiscatory taxation of large fortunes and inheritances.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Long did not propose a balanced budget; he proposed massive redistribution.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Foreign loans were not Long's funding mechanism.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The gold standard was irrelevant to Long's tax-the-rich funding.

items.stem: Which group would have been most likely to endorse the cartoon's perspective?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photograph by Lewis Hine, c. 1911 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: (A) Members of the New York State legislature depicted in the cartoon.
(B) Defenders of the 'cult of domesticity.'
(C) Members of the Progressive reform movement.
(D) Adherents of Social Darwinism.
items.explanation: The cartoon — presumably a Progressive-era image celebrating reform — would most likely be endorsed by members of the Progressive reform movement: the middle-class activists who fought for labor laws, suffrage, and social justice. They were the cartoon's natural audience and allies. Legislators, domesticity defenders, and Social Darwinists stood on the other side.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The legislators depicted as oppressors would not endorse the cartoon's critique.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Defenders of the cult of domesticity opposed the reforms the cartoon celebrates.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Progressive reformers would most likely endorse the cartoon's perspective.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Social Darwinists justified inequality; they would not endorse reformist sympathy.

items.stem: The statement above was most likely prompted by which of the following world events?

stimulus.text: “Whereas the laws and treaties of the United States, without interfering with the free expression of opinion and sympathy, or with the commercial manufacture or sale of arms or munitions of war, nevertheless impose upon all persons who may be within their territory and jurisdiction the duty of an impartial neutrality during the existence of the contest; And Whereas it is the duty of a neutral government not to permit or suffer the making of its waters subservient to the purposes of war…. “Now, Therefore, I, Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States of America, in order to preserve the neutrality of the United States…do hereby declare and proclaim…. “That the statutes and the treaties of the United States and the law of nations alike require that no person, within the territory and jurisdiction of the United States, shall take part, directly or indirectly, in the said wars, but shall remain at peace with all of the said belligerents, and shall maintain a strict and impartial neutrality….” Source: Woodrow Wilson, 1914

options: (A) Cuban revolt against Spanish control
(B) Adolph Hitler’s invasion of Poland
(C) Austria-Hungary declaring war on Serbia
(D) Mussolini’s invasion of Ethiopia
items.explanation: Wilson's 1914 neutrality proclamation — declaring strict and impartial neutrality — was prompted by the outbreak of World War I in Europe: Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia in July 1914, which cascaded into continental war. Wilson's statement was America's answer to the guns of August. The event was the war's beginning, not its later crises.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Cuba's revolt against Spain was 1898, sixteen years earlier.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Hitler's invasion of Poland was 1939, a different war.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia prompted Wilson's 1914 neutrality proclamation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Mussolini's Ethiopia invasion was 1935.

items.stem: [Image description: Victor Gillam, 'A Lesson for Anti-Expansionists,' Judge magazine, 1899 — a pro-expansion cartoon celebrating American overseas acquisitions.] The cartoon was most likely published in the immediate aftermath of which conflict?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Judge magazine, 1899 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: (A) The War of 1812.
(B) The Mexican-American War.
(C) The Spanish-American War.
(D) World War I.
items.explanation: Victor Gillam's 1899 Judge cartoon — A Lesson for Anti-Expansionists, celebrating American overseas acquisitions — was published in the immediate aftermath of the Spanish-American War. The war's victories in Cuba and the Philippines gave America its first colonies, and pro-expansion cartoons celebrated the new empire. The cartoon belongs to 1898's imperial moment.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The War of 1812 produced no overseas acquisitions to celebrate.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Mexican-American War was continental expansion, not 1899's overseas empire.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The cartoon followed the Spanish-American War's overseas acquisitions.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. World War I came two decades later.

items.stem: [Image description: C. D. Batchelor cartoon, New York Daily News, April 25, 1936 — an American figure tempted or threatened by the prospect of another European war.] The cartoon's point is which of the following?
options: (A) Though Europe might slide into another great war, the United States should stay out of it.
(B) Appeasement was a bankrupt policy that guaranteed more death and destruction.
(C) Munitions makers — the 'merchants of death' — were driving the world toward war for profit.
(D) Modern weapons had made future wars unimaginably deadly.
items.explanation: C. D. Batchelor's 1936 cartoon — an American figure tempted or threatened by another European war — makes the isolationist point: though Europe might slide into another great war, the United States should stay out of it. In 1936, with fascism rising, the cartoon voices the dominant American sentiment: Europe's wars are not ours. Stay out.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The cartoon's point is that the United States should stay out of Europe's coming war.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The cartoon does not condemn appeasement; it counsels noninvolvement.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Munitions makers are not the cartoon's subject.

items.stem: Which of the following rationales does Beveridge employ in his argument?

stimulus.text: “The Opposition tells us that we ought not to govern a people without their consent. I answer, the rule of liberty that all just government derives its authority from the consent of the governed, applies only to those who are capable of self-government. We govern the Indians without their consent, we govern our territories without their consent, we govern our children without their consent. How do they know that our government would be without their consent? Would not the people of the Philippines prefer the just, human, civilizing government of this Republic to the savage, bloody rule of pillage and extortion from which we have rescued them? And, regardless of this formula of words made only for enlightened, self-governing people, do we owe no duty to the world? Shall we turn these peoples back to the reeking hands from which we have taken them? Shall we abandon them, with Germany, England, Japan, hungering for them? Shall we save them from those nations, to give them a self-rule of tragedy?…Then like men and not like children, let us on to our tasks, our mission, and our destiny.” Source: Albert J. Beveridge, “The March of the Flag,” 1898

options: (A) The closing of the western frontier impels the United States to expand its territory overseas.
(B) Governing territories confers economic benefits to both European and non-white nations.
(C) Powerful nations have a moral duty to govern less-developed nations.
(D) Racial superiority confers responsibility to the United States and Europe over the affairs of developing nations.
items.explanation: Beveridge's March of the Flag argues that powerful nations have a moral duty to govern less-developed nations: America must rule the Philippines because Filipinos cannot rule themselves and because civilization demands it. The white man's burden in American dress — empire as moral obligation. Beveridge's rationale is duty, not profit or strategy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The closing frontier is Turner's thesis, not Beveridge's rationale.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Economic benefits to both sides are not Beveridge's argument; moral duty is.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Beveridge argues powerful nations have a moral duty to govern less-developed nations.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Beveridge speaks of civilizing mission, not explicitly of racial superiority conferring responsibility.

questions.stimulus_text: With the Cold War over, historians argue, the 1990s became the decade of globalization: markets, culture, and information flowed across borders with unprecedented speed. dbq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the American state can be described as imperialist from 1890 to 1945.

documents.text:
In 1862, when the United States was involved in the War of the Rebellion, the Europeans took advantage of the situation to invade Mexico, and to establish there a 'stable government.' They undertook to protect that people against themselves, and to erect for them a species of protectorate, such as we now propose for the Philippines. As soon as our war was over, we insisted upon the withdrawal of Europe from Mexico. What followed is matter of recent history. It is unnecessary to recall it. We did not reduce Mexico into a condition of 'tutelage,' or establish over it a 'protectorate' of our own. We, on the contrary, insisted that it should stand on its own legs; and, by so doing, learn to stand firmly on them, just as a child learns to walk, by being compelled to try to walk, not by being kept everlastingly in 'leading strings.' This was the American, as contradistinguished from the European policy; and Mexico to-day walks firmly.

Finally take the case of Venezuela in 1895. I believe I am not mistaken when I say that, during the twenty-five preceding years, Venezuela had undergone almost as many revolutions. It certainly had not enjoyed a stable government. Through disputes over questions of boundary, Great Britain proposed to confer that indisputable blessing upon a considerable region. We interfered under a most questionable extension of the Monroe Doctrine, and asserted the principle of 'Hands-off.' Having done this - having in so far perpetuated what we now call the scandal of anarchy - we did not establish 'tutelage,' or a protectorate, ourselves. We wisely left Venezuela to work out its destiny in its own way, and in the fullness of time. That policy was far-seeing, beneficent, and strictly American in 1895. Why, then, make almost indecent haste to abandon it in 1898?

Instead, therefore, of finding our precedents in the experience of England, or that of any other European power, I would suggest that the true course for this country now to pursue is exactly the course we have heretofore pursued under similar conditions. Let us be true to our own traditions, and follow our own precedents. Having relieved the Spanish islands from the dominion of Spain, we should declare concerning them a policy of 'Hands-off,' both on our own part and on the part of other powers.
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Charles Francis Adams, Jr., historian and great-grandson of John Adams, letter to Hon. Carl Schurz. POV: elite anti-imperialist. Purpose: persuade against Philippine annexation by appealing to American precedent. Audience: fellow anti-imperialist. Argument relevance: articulates the anti-imperialist case from American tradition - evidence against the imperialist label.

documents.text:
In the United States, the imperialist war waged against Spain in 1898 stirred up the opposition of the 'anti-imperialists,' the last of the Mohicans of bourgeois democracy. They declared this war to be 'criminal'; denounced the annexation of foreign territories as being a violation of the constitution, and they denounced the 'jingo treachery' by means of which Aguinaldo, leader of the rebel native Filipinos, was deceived (first the Americans promised him the independence of his country; then they landed troops and annexed it). They quoted the words of Lincoln: 'It is self-government when the white man governs himself; but when he governs himself and also governs others, it is no longer self-government, it is despotism.'

But all this criticism shrank from recognizing the indissoluble bond between imperialism and the trusts, and, therefore, between imperialism and the very foundations of capitalism....
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Vladimir Lenin, Imperialism: The Last Stage of Capitalism. POV: Marxist revolutionary. Purpose: theoretical critique linking imperialism to capitalism. Audience: socialists. Argument relevance: external ideological critique framing American expansion as capitalist imperialism - supports the imperialist label from a hostile witness.

The Philippine Islands are west of the United States, and near the southern coast of Asia.... The Island of Luzon, on which the capital city, Manila, is located, is about the size of New York State....

The published statements of W.B. Wilcox, Paymaster, U.S. Navy, and Ensign L.R. Sargent, U.S. Navy, who, in 1898, made a visit to the most distant districts of the Island of Luzon, are highly commendable to the character and ability of the natives whom they met and associated with.

They were cordial and honorable in their treatment of our men at that time, and these people were found to be comfortably situated, and enjoying life since the departure of the Spaniards. They are an intelligent and a polite people; ambitious to improve their condition every way. They are patriotic and high-minded, as described by these officers, and while they may have since entertained a mistaken idea regarding our intentions towards them, and given us battle, they are capable of being won over to a brotherly regard for our people.

With proper care and direction, these people will become happy, and a strength to our nation. There should be no desire to, in the least, encroach upon their property....

Purpose: promote benevolent assimilation of the Philippines. Audience: American public. Argument relevance: paternalistic justification of empire - 'proper care and direction' of Filipinos reveals the imperial mindset behind annexation.

Territories and possessions exclusive of the Philippines totaled 2,477,023 people in 1940, up from 1,680,202 in 1920.

documents.text: Described from a political cartoon by Victor Gillam in Judge magazine (1899), titled 'A Thing Well Begun Is Half Done.' President McKinley, sleeves rolled up, digs with a shovel at Central America beside a sign reading 'Proposed Nicaragua Canal,' while Uncle Sam carries rifles past the Capitol. American flags fly over the Philippines, Hawaii, Cuba, and Porto Rico. The caption reads: 'Uncle Sam - "Finish the canal, McKinley, and make our national expansion complete in your first administration."'
documents.sourcing_note: POV: pro-expansion popular magazine. Purpose: urge McKinley to complete the canal and national expansion. Audience: magazine readers. Argument relevance: shows popular imperialist enthusiasm - expansion celebrated as a national project, evidence for the imperialist description.

section_2b.directions: Section II, Part B — Long Essay: 1 question, 40 minutes. Develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, and support your argument with specific and relevant examples. This part counts for 15 percent of the exam score. Total exam time: 3 hours 15 minutes.

leq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which differing economies shaped differing social structures in the English colonies in North America.
leq.guidance: Thesis frame: argue how New England, Middle, and Southern economies produced distinct social orders. Evidence buckets: Southern plantation slavery and planter hierarchy; New England town-based, mixed-farming society; Middle Colony diversity and commerce; indentured servitude vs. enslaved labor.
